opus-5.5.text:
I think of it as a continuum rather than separate stages. People used to draw a hard line: pre-training on a huge web corpus to learn the world, then post-training with SFT and RLHF to teach behavior. In practice, that boundary has blurred a lot, and continual pre-training sits right in the middle.

Once you have a base model, you often want it to get much better at code, math, long context, or a new language. You don't restart from scratch; you keep training on a data mixture that shifts toward what you care about. That shift is a kind of soft alignment. You're telling the model which part of the distribution matters, which is conceptually what post-training does, just with a weaker, broader signal.

What I find really interesting is the annealing phase at the end of pre-training. You lower the learning rate and upsample high-quality data, sometimes including synthetic or instruction-like data. That's where you see big jumps on benchmarks, and it changes what's easy to elicit afterwards. If the model has already seen reasoning traces or well-structured answers during annealing, post-training has much less to teach. It's more about unlocking and shaping than injecting new knowledge.

So I'd frame it like this: pre-training gives you capabilities, post-training gives you behavior and preferences, and continual pre-training is how you move the capability frontier in the direction post-training will need. The better you design that middle stage, the more RL and human feedback can focus on what they're uniquely good at, which is going beyond imitation, rather than patching gaps the data should have covered.

There's a practical side too. Continual pre-training lets you refresh knowledge, extend context, or specialize without paying full pre-training cost. As post-training compute grows, especially with RL, I expect these stages to keep merging, with a dial between "learn from data" and "learn from feedback" instead of discrete phases.

r001.rationale: It says continual pre-training can specialize a model in areas such as code, math, long context, or a new language, developing expertise in those domains.

r002.rationale: It says continual pre-training lets RL and human feedback focus on their strengths, but does not state that domain expertise enables collecting higher-quality RLHF annotations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions right now, because the boundary between pre-training and post-training is becoming much more blurry than it used to be.

Historically you had this very clean separation. You pre-train on trillions of tokens of web data, you get a base model, and then post-training is this small, almost artisanal phase at the end where you do SFT and RLHF to make the model usable. And the mental model was that pre-training gives you the knowledge and the capabilities, and post-training just surfaces them, aligns them, teaches the model the format of a conversation.

I think that picture is wrong now, or at least incomplete. What we saw with Llama 2 and even more with Llama 3 is that post-training is where a lot of the capability actually gets shaped. And continual pre-training is the bridge, because it lets you keep injecting data at scale, with the same objective as pre-training, but with a distribution that's much closer to what you want the model to do at the end.

So concretely, you can think of it as a curriculum. Early pre-training is very broad, very noisy, you just want coverage. Then as you go, you anneal, you shift the data mixture toward higher quality, toward more code, more math, more reasoning traces, more synthetic data. And by the end, the data you're training on with next-token prediction already looks a lot like post-training data. The model is basically being prepared for the behaviors you want before you even start the alignment stage.

And the other direction is important too. Post-training generates a lot of signal, you learn what the model is bad at, where the reward model disagrees with it, which domains are weak. That feeds back into what you continue pre-training on. So it becomes a loop rather than a pipeline. You can take a model that's already been post-trained, generate synthetic data from it, filter with a verifier or a reward model, and put that back into continual pre-training to push the base further.

I'd also say continual pre-training is what makes the whole thing economically sane. You don't want to retrain from scratch every time you have a better data recipe or a new domain you care about. You want to keep the base and keep moving it. And that forces you to think about things like learning rate schedules, how you avoid catastrophic forgetting, how you mix in replay from the original distribution. Those are pre-training problems, but you're solving them in service of post-training goals.

So for me, the honest answer is that in a year or two I'm not sure we'll even talk about them as two separate stages. It will be one long training run where the objective and the data distribution evolve continuously, and "post-training" just means the last part of that curve where the signal gets denser and more targeted.

r001.rationale: The response describes continual pre-training as shifting training toward specific areas such as code, math, and reasoning, and as continuing training for a new domain the model needs—communicating domain expertise development.

r002.rationale: It mentions RLHF and reward-model feedback, but does not state that domain expertise from continual pre-training enables collecting higher-quality RLHF annotations.

astra-6.text:
I think continual pre-training blurs the boundary between pre-training and post-training. We tend to describe them as separate stages: first you acquire knowledge by predicting the next token, and then you teach the model how to behave. But you can keep training the model on new data, including data that reflects the capabilities or behaviors you want to improve.

The interesting question becomes: what data do you introduce, and with what objective? You might use a pre-training objective to incorporate new knowledge, then instruction tuning or reinforcement learning to make that knowledge useful in an interaction. Those are complementary processes.

And ideally, that becomes a loop. You deploy a model, identify where it struggles, and use that information to inform the next round of training. Continual pre-training is part of the bridge, but the challenge is making those updates without losing capabilities the model already has.

r001.rationale: The response says continual pre-training can incorporate new knowledge, but does not identify it as a way to develop domain expertise.

r002.rationale: The response mentions reinforcement learning, but does not connect domain expertise to collecting higher-quality RLHF annotations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think continual pre-training blurs the boundary between pre-training and post-training. We tend to describe them as separate stages: first you learn from a huge amount of text, then you teach the model to follow instructions or solve tasks. But you can keep updating that same model with new knowledge, new capabilities, and feedback.

The interesting question is what you train on next. If you discover a weakness during post-training, can you bring in the right data and address it through continued training, without losing what the model already knows? Then it becomes a loop: train, evaluate, identify what’s missing, and train again. In that sense, continual pre-training is a bridge toward a model that keeps improving, rather than one whose learning is divided into a few fixed stages.

r001.rationale: It describes adding knowledge and capabilities through continued training, but does not identify developing domain expertise as a contribution.

r002.rationale: It mentions feedback but does not state that domain expertise enables higher-quality RLHF annotations.
